summary:
This run covered 10 evals; two (negative-provisioned-throughput-sizing, neg-endpoint-latency) were "should_trigger: false" scenarios and correctly skipped for both variants (both show trigger_fired 1/1, meaning neither falsely engaged — a consistent, positive result with no variant difference to report). The remaining 8 evals form the basis of comparison.

Across these 8 evals, trigger_fired was 1/1 (100%) in every case, so the behavior under test reliably fired for both variants.

On "met expected output," with_skill passed 7 of 8 evals (all but none skipped) while without_skill passed in 6 of 8, failing outright on "evaluation-coverage-assessment" (0/1, medium confidence) and "finish-reason-truncation-drift" (0/1, high confidence). In the other 6 evals both variants met the expected output.

Per-assertion pass rates favored with_skill in most evals, sometimes substantially: e.g. evaluation-coverage-assessment (with_skill 5/6 vs without_skill 1/6), finish-reason-truncation-drift (4/5 vs 1/5), output-contract-drift (7/8 vs 4/8), qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression (7/7 vs 5/7), se-eval-job-failed (7/7 vs 1/7). In qe-baseline-missing, without_skill was ahead (4/4 vs 3/4), and in qe-regression-gate-missing with_skill was slightly ahead (4/4 vs 3/4). In se-never-evaluated, both variants tied at 3/7, and several assertions failed for both variants in that eval (risk-of-shipping-without-evaluation, SageMaker-specific job-type check, no-raw-account-ID), indicating gaps in the underlying behavior or assertion design rather than a variant-specific issue.

Several individual assertions show patterns worth noting on their own: some always pass for both variants (e.g., "explains production-safety consequence," "names concrete cause," "requires baseline," various generic-advice checks) — these don't differentiate the variants. Others always fail for both (e.g., distinguishing "no eval configured" vs "region unsupported," citing SageMaker-specific check behavior, avoiding raw account ID exposure in se-never-evaluated) — these point to shared weaknesses rather than one variant underperforming. A clear number of assertions follow a "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern, especially around citing check-IDs, marking thresholds as workload-specific/derived, and citing baselines — but a couple go the other way (without_skill passes "explicit that retrospective comparison may not be possible" in qe-baseline-missing; without_skill favored on accuracy/actionability for qe-regression-gate-missing and se-eval-job-failed quality comparisons).

On quality comparisons (LLM-judged, limited pairs: 0 or 1 per eval, several skipped for lack of data), with_skill was favored overall in most of the 6 evals where quality comparison ran (output-contract-drift, qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression, qe-baseline-missing, se-never-evaluated, se-eval-job-failed showed with_skill favored on 2–3 of 3 criteria), while qe-regression-gate-missing favored without_skill on 1 of 3 criteria (actionability) with the rest comparable, and se-eval-job-failed showed a mixed picture (with_skill favored on 2 criteria, without_skill on accuracy). These are based on only one evaluated pair each, so confidence is limited (mostly "medium"), and two evals (evaluation-coverage-assessment, finish-reason-truncation-drift) had quality comparisons skipped entirely (0 pairs evaluated), so no quality signal exists there.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was consistently much faster and cheaper — in several evals (finish-reason-truncation-drift, output-contract-drift, qe-regression-gate-missing, se-eval-job-failed) without_skill's runtime and cost registered as 0s/$0.00, versus with_skill's 18–39s and $0.15–$0.37. Where without_skill did register runtime (evaluation-coverage-assessment, qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression, qe-baseline-missing, se-never-evaluated), it still ran roughly 2-4x faster and cheaper than with_skill (e.g., 14s/$0.12 vs 58s/$0.48). This is a substantial and consistent efficiency difference in without_skill's favor, which contrasts with with_skill's generally higher assertion pass rates and quality-comparison scores — a tradeoff rather than a clear overall verdict.

Output consistency across repeated runs was not measured (null) for either variant in any eval, so no run-to-run stability data is available to weigh.

Overall, the results show with_skill meeting more individual assertions and being favored more often in limited-sample quality comparisons, while without_skill runs and costs substantially less across nearly all evals. Confidence on quality differences is capped by very small sample sizes (0-1 pairs per eval) and medium-level confidence ratings; several assertions and two full evals (quality comparisons) lack any differentiating signal at all.

output-contract-drift.summary:

On the finer-grained assertion checks (8 total), with_skill passed 7/8 (88%) and without_skill passed 4/8 (50%). Breaking this down:
- Three assertions passed for both variants (always_passes): recommending a concrete way to quantify parse-failure/schema-deviation rates, recommending a non-voluntary enforcement mechanism (e.g., schema validation), and recommending a durable detection mechanism rather than a one-off fix. Also, both variants considered an undocumented model update as a candidate cause (always passes). These shared successes aren't differentiating.
- One assertion failed for both variants (always_fails): citing an evaluation check-id. This indicates either the assertion or the expected behavior may not be well-supported by either variant's output, rather than a variant-specific weakness.
- Three assertions passed for with_skill but failed for without_skill: requiring a pre-change baseline to distinguish a genuine shift from normal model non-determinism; noting dependency on Bedrock model invocation logging (and reporting whether it's enabled); and framing the regression-gate margin as workload-specific rather than an AWS-published threshold. The last of these had only "low" confidence on without_skill's failing side, so that specific finding is less certain; the other two were medium/high confidence.

On quality comparison (only one pair evaluated, so this is a single data point, not a trend), with_skill was favored on accuracy and actionability, with completeness rated comparable between the two. Overall this gave with_skill 2 favorable criterion outcomes versus 0 for without_skill, at medium average confidence.

On cost and runtime, with_skill took ~32s and cost ~$0.27 on average, while without_skill shows 0s runtime and $0.00 cost — this looks like no meaningful work/cost was recorded for without_skill in this run rather than a genuine instantaneous free response, so these metrics should be treated cautiously rather than as a real efficiency advantage. The runtime comparison notes 1 of 1 evaluated pairs exceeded the 30s threshold (attributable to with_skill's ~32s runtime), at high confidence. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.4% vs 4.4%), with no compaction events for either.

No output-consistency data is available for either variant (both null), so repeat-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-pair evaluation with some low-confidence or missing data points (notably without_skill's expected-output confidence, the low-confidence regression-gate assertion, and the suspect zero-cost/zero-runtime metrics for without_skill). Within that limited evidence, with_skill showed higher assertion pass rates and was favored on the quality comparisons that were run, while without_skill's recorded runtime/cost were lower (though likely not meaningfully comparable given the 0s/$0.00 values). Both variants shared several passing and one failing assertion, which do not differentiate them.

Consistency: Output consistency data (variance across repeated runs) is null/absent for both variants, so no conclusion can be drawn about run-to-run stability for either.

Overall picture: On this single-task evaluation, with_skill showed higher assertion pass rates and was favored in the (limited, medium-confidence) quality comparison, while without_skill ran notably faster and cheaper. This represents a speed/cost versus completeness/quality-signal tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome, and the small sample size (one pair) and medium-confidence quality judgments mean these differences should be treated as preliminary rather than conclusive.
